title: CONGENITAL MYOPATHY 10B, MILD VARIANT
alt_titles: MYOPATHY, AREFLEXIA, RESPIRATORY DISTRESS, AND DYSPHAGIA, EARLY-ONSET, MILD VARIANT

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital myopathy-10B, mild variant (CMYO10B), is caused by compound heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the MEGF10 gene (612453) on chromosome 5q23.

paragraphs.text: Takayama et al. (2016) noted that mutations in the MEGF10 gene cause early-onset myopathy with areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (EMARDD). They also cause a milder phenotype of minicore myopathy. Features of the milder form include weakness beginning in infancy or childhood that is mainly axial and proximal, facial weakness, contractures, scoliosis, hypernasal speech, palatal abnormalities, and respiratory involvement. Muscle biopsy shows minicores and dystrophic features (Boyden et al., 2012).

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) described a non-consanguineous Caucasian family of mixed European ancestry (family 1030) in which 3 of 4 sibs had an autosomal recessive myopathy that resembled multiminicore disease in some respects. Weakness began by 12 months of age, first in the neck. It was mainly axial and proximal, included facial weakness, and stabilized in adolescence. The patients had neck contractures in infancy and elbow, knee, and heel cord contractures by adulthood. Serum CK was mildly elevated. All 3 had childhood-onset scoliosis treated with spinal fusion, and respiratory problems from age 10 to 11 years that were treated with nocturnal BiPAP. All 3 had hypernasal speech; 1 had a cleft palate and another had a midline palatal ridge. Muscle biopsies showed dystrophic features: myofibers replaced by fat, increased perimysial and endomysial connective tissue, and isolated regenerating fibers. They also showed moth-eaten fibers and minicores, which suggested a congenital myopathy, and a slight predominance of type I fibers. Rimmed vacuoles, inclusions, central cores, nemaline rods, and ragged red fibers were absent.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) also described a girl (subject 105-1), a Caucasian with distant Portuguese ancestry, who had been diagnosed with multiminicore disease and had no affected relatives. At several weeks of age she had hypotonia with a weak neck, a markedly high-arched palate, failure to thrive from poor feeding, blue sclerae, and hyperflexible joints. In childhood she had frequent pulmonary infections but no chronic breathing problems. Serum CK was 302 U/L at age 10, and her scoliosis had progressed to 20 degrees by age 12. Muscle biopsy showed minicores, which were confirmed by electron microscopy.

paragraphs.text: Croci et al. (2022) reported a 22-year-old Italian man born to healthy consanguineous parents. He was born at 33 weeks' gestation, needed resuscitation for asphyxia at birth, and had a weak suck. Elbow contractures and scoliosis were present from the first months of life. He had no motor developmental delay or intellectual disability. He later developed slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, dysphagia, and respiratory involvement, and he needed nocturnal noninvasive ventilation from age 16 years. On examination he had axial hypotonia, generalized muscle hypotrophy and weakness, preserved facial expression, cleft palate, global areflexia, bilateral elbow and ankle contractures, equinovarus foot stance, and hyperlordosis. Serum CK, brain and spine MRI, ECG, and echocardiogram were normal. From age 17 he had swallowing difficulties and recurrent aspiration pneumonia. A quadriceps muscle biopsy at age 5 years showed nonspecific changes: variation in fiber size, internal nuclei, and fibrosis. A later biopsy showed myofibrillar changes, including whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions, and minicores. Electrophysiology showed normal conduction apart from reduced amplitudes of muscle evoked potentials. The authors proposed that the minicores seen in the late-onset group may result from a long-standing myofibrillar process that begins in infancy.

paragraphs.text: In the 3 affected sibs of family 1030 with a myopathy resembling multiminicore disease, Boyden et al. (2012) used linkage-filtered whole genome sequencing to identify compound heterozygous missense mutations in the MEGF10 gene. The mutations were C326R and C774R. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the mutations were in trans and segregated with the disease. Both mutations were absent from public databases and from genotyped controls. Boyden et al. (2012) also sequenced MEGF10 in 190 patients with unexplained myopathies. One patient (subject 105-1) was heterozygous for an R71W mutation inherited from an unaffected parent. No second mutation was found by cDNA sequencing, and the patient had no SEPN1 or RYR1 mutations. The authors suggested that she may carry a second MEGF10 mutation they were unable to detect. In zebrafish, knockdown of megf10 produced a myopathic phenotype, which the authors took as support for the pathogenicity of the human mutations.

checks.claim: The MEGF10 C699S variant was absent from ClinVar and gnomAD.
checks.evidence_quote: This variant is absent in genomic databases (such as ClinVar and gnomAD)

checks.claim: The MEGF10 C699S variant affects a conserved residue in an EGF-like domain.
checks.evidence_quote: the novel homozygous variant p.Cys699S affecting a very conserved cysteine residue in a crucial EGF-like functional domain.

checks.claim: The MEGF10 C699S variant was predicted to be damaging by in silico tools.
checks.evidence_quote: is predicted to be pathogenic by several in silico tools, including CADD (27.9), Mutation Taster (disease causing, score = 1), SIFT4G (damaging, score = 0.001), and Polyphen-2 HVAR (damaging, score = 0.99).

checks.claim: The MEGF10 C699S variant was classified as likely pathogenic under ACMG criteria.
checks.evidence_quote: This amino acid change is further classified as likely pathogenic according to the ACMG criteria (PM2, PP3).

checks.claim: No functional studies of the MEGF10 C699S variant were done.
checks.evidence_quote: Functional studies are warranted to confirm the role and pathogenetic association of MEGF10 mutation in our patient.
checks.explanation: The paper says functional studies are still needed, which implies none were done.

allelic_variants.name: MEGF10, 2-BP DEL, 131_132
allelic_variants.phenotype: Early-onset myopathy, areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (severe EMARDD)

paragraphs.text: In a Japanese patient with the severe EMARDD phenotype, Takayama et al. (2016) identified a homozygous frameshift mutation (c.131_132del) in the MEGF10 gene. They contrasted this patient with a second Japanese patient who had the milder phenotype and compound heterozygous mutations including a cysteine missense mutation, and concluded that the findings indicated a genotype-phenotype correlation in MEGF10 myopathy.

checks.claim: Takayama et al. (2016) studied a Japanese patient with the severe EMARDD phenotype.
checks.evidence_quote: one with EMARDD phenotype who had a novel homozygous frameshift mutation, c.131_132del

checks.claim: In a Japanese patient with the severe EMARDD phenotype, Takayama et al. (2016) identified a homozygous frameshift mutation (c.131_132del) in the MEGF10 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: one with EMARDD phenotype who had a novel homozygous frameshift mutation, c.131_132del

checks.claim: Takayama et al. (2016) compared the severe EMARDD patient with a second Japanese patient who had the milder phenotype and compound heterozygous MEGF10 mutations, including a cysteine missense mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: This is the first report on East Asian patients with MEGF10 myopathy showing two phenotypes, indicating the genotype-phenotype correlation in MEGF10 myopathy.
checks.explanation: The paper presents both patients side by side to show two phenotypes. The second patient's milder phenotype and compound heterozygous cysteine missense mutation are stated.

checks.claim: Takayama et al. (2016) concluded that their findings showed a genotype-phenotype correlation in MEGF10 myopathy.
checks.evidence_quote: indicating the genotype-phenotype correlation in MEGF10 myopathy.
